utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. Appearing for the Prosecution today Mark Harmon and Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone. Today Mr. Perisic is represented by Novak Lukic and Gregor Guy-Smith as Defence counsel. And our legal assistants are here, Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, and Chad Mair as well as our case manager, Daniela Tasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Court go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I can call the next witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise to Counsel. Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can call the next witness, Mr. Milan Gunj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Thank you. Mr. Harmon will explain one or two things in relation to your protective measures to you before you start. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In -- you are testifying publicly, but in the course of your public testimony, we will go into private session briefly on a few occasions. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Right. Sir, could you state your name, please, and spell your last name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: G-u-n-j. That is my last name. And my first name is M-i-l-a-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I'm a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long have you been a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Since 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And prior to becoming a professional soldier, do you have any relationship to the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I did. Starting in 1985, I was a civilian working in the army as the chief cook.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how was it that you transitioned from being a civilian employee in the army to becoming an active soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Probably my work, the way I carried out all my tasks, all this was viewed in such a way that I was offered this opportunity which I took.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what specifically from 1992 to the present time have been your duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Starting from 1992 until 1997 I was in charge of military restaurants and canteens. As of 1997, I have been the administrator of the military vacation home at Rajac where I still am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll come to that subject in just a minute, Mr. Gunj. Prior to coming to testify in these proceedings, did you provide a statement on the 24th of March 2006 before an investigative judge in the 2nd municipal Court in Belgrade as part of criminal proceedings against a particular accused person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you also provide a statement before Judge Plazinic in the Belgrade district court war crimes Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In those proceedings, Mr. Gunj, you were summoned to the war crimes Chamber, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to Judge Plazinic, those were proceedings that were conducted in my presence, in the presence of Mr. Bretton Randall who was an investigator from my office and in the presence of Mr. Novak Lukic who is the Defence counsel for General Perisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you returning to your duties in -- as an administrator at the vacation home at Rajac. First of all, can you explain going back to 1997 what was the hotel at Rajac? What function did it serve? And what condition was it in?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: When I took over my duty in 1997, the facility was in rather poor condition. It occasionally functioned for the official needs of the Army of Yugoslavia, but only from time to time because it did not have sufficient professional staff, and it was not sufficiently well equipped to be able to function properly over a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was the facility at Rajac a facility that was under the jurisdiction and authority of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How far away from Belgrade was this particular facility?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Between 90 and 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was it a facility that was open to the public?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Not at that time. It wasn't at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you also -- did the Hotel Topcider also come within your authority and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Initially when I took over my duty that was the case. I was also responsible for the Topcider hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, can you explain to Their Honours what was the hotel Topcider, what condition it was in.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: The Topcider hotel was in much better condition than the Rajac hotel at the time I assumed my duties because professional soldiers working in the army and their families lived there, so it operated better than the Rajac hotel. It was a facility of the closed type. It was not open to the public, and it was within a barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this then was a facility also under the authority of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was it a secure facility? In other words, in order to gain access to it, did you have to do anything particularly to get access to it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: You had to come to the main gate of the Topcider barracks within which the hotel was, that was the first check you had to go through. And then when entering the hotel itself, there was also a small porter's desk where the people who lived inside and the people who came to visit were checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which town is this Topcider hotel?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That was my next question, Your Honour. That's quite all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you answer Judge Moloto's question, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: In Belgrade. It's in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was this facility located on an army base?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, in an army base in a barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And then I would like to turn -- direct your attention to a third facility. A facility at Stragari. Can you, first of all, tell me whether and under whose authority the facility at Stragari was, and what the facility was.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: This facility was also under the jurisdiction of the Army of Yugoslavia. It was used for the needs of the army but not for tourism. It was far larger than the Rajac hotel. It had more room inside. More space.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how far away from Belgrade was that located?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Between 70 and 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that a facility that was open to the public, or was it a secure facility?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: It was not open to the public, and it was secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "secure," in order to gain access to that facility, what did you have to do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: You mean Stragari?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: You would get to the gate and there would be a duty officer to check you, and then you would be given a badge which would give you permission to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, under which command did the facilities that you've just described, the hotel Topcider, the hotel Rajac and Stragari, under which command did they fall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: They were under the command of the staff administration of the command of the 1st Army of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did the unit to which you belonged have a military post number designating it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: You mean the three buildings, that the three facilities belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about a designation for the unit in which you belonged? MP and then some number to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did this witness belong to a unit, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, that's -- he will, Your Honour, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that the first question. My problem -- having listened to the evidence so far, it looks like he has just been working in the catering system of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, did you belong to a unit in the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did belong to a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what was your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: It was military post 2082 through 31, and it was the headquarters administration of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, could you identify your chain of command, first identifying your superior officer by name. And I'm talking in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the commander of military post 2082/31, Colonel Momcilo Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And going up the chain of command from Colonel Jovanovic, who was his superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Colonel Jovanovic's immediate superior was the Chief of Staff of the deputy of the commander of the 1st Army, General Marjanovic, and then the next up the chain was General Trajkovic who was the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And above General Trajkovic, who was his superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: According to our military hierarchy, evidently it was the chief of the General Staff because the commander of the 1st Army, as far as I know, is immediately subordinate to the chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And who was that person, who was the chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: At the time the chief of the General Staff was General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention to events that took place in late June or early July of 1997. At that time, Mr. Gunj, were you the manager of the hotel at Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did something unusual happen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Well, what happened was that one day in the evening some guests arrived in the hotel unannounced, and they were received by the soldier who was there at the time on duty. He rang me up and informed me that some guests had arrived and that he couldn't tell me anything more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you said, Mr. Gunj, that somebody rang you up. An employee of the hotel, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes. He was an employee. His name was Pasojovic. He was a contract soldier, a professional soldier at the time, and he rang me up personally. I was in Belgrade. I was at my home in Belgrade at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And after being informed that there were guests at this facility, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I asked that one of the guests talk to me so that I could see what this was about because this soldier evidently didn't dare or couldn't tell me what this was about. After that, a gentleman surnamed Banduka spoke to me, but he couldn't explain what this was about either. He asked me to go there. That was the end of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he give you any other instructions or give you any other information before you went to the hotel at Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: You have them in mind, the people from the hotel, do you have the telephone call in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, did Mr. Banduka inform you of anything prior to your leaving to go to the hotel at Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Banduka didn't inform me of any details in particular, but he said that everything was fine, that it would be fine when I arrived there, and that I would see what the situation was. Ten minutes later, the phone rang again. There was a male voice that I heard on the other end. He didn't introduce himself. All I know is that he asked me whether he was Mr. Gunj, cabinet of the General Staff, go to the facility and there are guests there, and you will see what it's all about. Afterwards, I got into a vehicle and went to the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just clarify what you are evidence is on this point. What was translated to me and what is on the record, Mr. Gunj, is "he didn't introduce himself, all I know is that he asked me whether he was Mr. Gunj, cabinet of the General Staff, go to the facility." Let's clarify precisely what happened. When you received a phone call from this man, did he identify himself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No. He did not introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he identify from where he was calling?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: He said, I need Mr. Gunj. I said speaking. It's the office of the General Staff, go to the facility. And when you get there, you'll see what is the situation is. You have guests, they will see who your guests are. And that was what we spoke about. I said fine, I packed very rapidly and set off to the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how long did it take you to get to the facility?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Usually it takes about two hours of normal driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And when you arrived, Mr. Gunj, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: When I arrived at the gate, I saw some men in civilian clothing there. Some of them were armed. They were standing aside. The person who approached me did not introduce himself, but they behaved correctly. I wanted them to tell me what was going on. He said go to the hotel, they'll provide you with explanations there. Don't be afraid. Everything is fine. And that is what was said at the gate when I first had contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you ever able to determine the identity of the person who said "it's the office of the General Staff, go to the facility, and when you get there you'll see what is the situation"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't able to do that. I haven't been able to do that to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, did this man who had identified himself, did he -- was he any more precise when he said that he was calling from the General Staff? Was he any more precise or descriptive when he contacted you during that initial telephone call?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I've already said that the gentleman did not introduce himself, and the conversation was very brief. Are you Mr. Gunj, I said yes. Go to Rajac, get prepared, and when you arrive there you'll see that you have guests. And that was the extent of the conversation. Good-bye, good-bye. There were no details presented. I didn't put any questions to this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yesterday when I was -- when we met to review your evidence, did you inform me that the person identified himself as being from the cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: The person did not introduce himself, but he said that he was phoning from the office of the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you arrived at the gate in -- upon going to Rajac, you said there were people who were in civilian clothes and who were armed. Approximately how many people did you see on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Well, there were these people who awaited me at the gate, and there were people who were there when I went down to the hotel, but there were 10 or 15 altogether. I can't be precise, but there were about 10 or 15 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you notice any vehicles in or around the facility?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, I saw some vehicles by the facility, on the compound of the military facility itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many vehicles did you observe?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Well, in my assessment between five and seven vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you look at the licence plates on those cars or vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: On the whole, the vehicles were civilian ones, and as far as I can remember, the licence plates were from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, after you --

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: At least the ones I saw. It was already dark, so I couldn't see all of them. But when I first arrived there, I noticed that the licence plates on some of them were civilian ones and from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, after you arrived at the facility, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: When I arrived at the main facility in the compound, I asked certain individuals who were at the gate, I didn't know them, but they were in civilian clothing too. I asked them what was going on. They said wait at the entrance, the boss wants to see you so that you can get to know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: And then I think Rajko Banduka was the first person to come out of the hotel. We met and then General Mladic followed him soon after, and we introduced ourselves to each other. I was somewhat surprised, scared, and confused by this turn of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And why were you scared or surprised by that turn of events?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Well, for a number of reasons. First of all, because this happened in my compound, and I had no information that this would happen so it was a surprise event. And secondly, I know that Mr. Ratko Mladic has been accused of certain acts by The Hague Tribunal. And at that point in time I was a state of panic. I was very afraid. I felt uneasy. How is it that this happened in my backyard, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how did you know that Mr. -- General Mladic had been accused by the Tribunal of certain crimes? How did you become aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Well, I knew just as everyone else did from the media, from the newspapers, from digital media. This is something that was known. It's not as if I had any particular access to such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before you actually met General Mladic that evening, you said you met Banduka first; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Correct. Banduka was the first person to come out of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself, did he have a complete name or first name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes. I'm Rajko Banduka. We spoke to each other on the phone awhile ago, and then I realised that this was the person who had called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he identify himself by rank?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No, not initially, he didn't mention his rank initially, but later I found out that he had the rank of a lieutenant through conversations with other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he, Mr. Gunj, have an accent that was different from accents that you hear in and around Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, he had a slightly Bosnian accent. That's where he was born. But it wasn't that pronounced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And before he -- before you met General Mladic, did you and Lieutenant Banduka discuss anything in particular that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No. This only took a minute, no more than that. He came out and then he was followed by General Mladic. We introduced ourselves to each other, and there weren't any subjects that were discuss. Not at all. There wasn't even time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what did -- tell the Judges about your encounter with General Mladic, your first encounter with him. How did that pass?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Well, he came out, I was standing outside on the terrace. He asked me, are you the person in charge here. I said yes. Do you know me? Do you know who I am? I said yes. He embraced me, and we walked around a bit. He said don't be afraid. Everything will be fine. That's how this encounter passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After you talked to General Mladic, did you again talk to Lieutenant Banduka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I then participated in the discussion on accommodation, et cetera. We found some other keys because the soldier who contacted me couldn't open up all the rooms. I showed them some facilities that could be used for accommodation because I could see what the situation was like. It was necessary to find accommodation so that everything could function properly. So that was the subject of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about provisions or supplies that were available at the facility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I refrained from intervening. I think my colleague Mr. Harmon is putting a leading question to the witness. On page 19, line 9, he said did you meet Banduka again, and then he says what did you talk about, were there any discussions about this. I think he should ask the witness an open question and then the witness can say what happened. But I think that phrasing the question this way amounts to putting a leading question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think agree that that is a leading question. Was there any discussion about provisions or supplies that were available at the facility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You can answer the question, Mr. Gunj. If you'd like, I can repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: At that time after I had seen General Mladic, I and Rajko Banduka discussed technical issues, accommodation, et cetera. We didn't immediately discuss the subjects of provision, the supplies because for that evening they had basic supplies, so we didn't discuss the subject of provisions right at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you discuss the issue of provisions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: On the following day, in the morning. We then had a more detailed discussion about all the relevant issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can you relate to Their Honours that discussion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Well, on the whole Banduka told me that they had a waiter of their own and a cook who would prepare and provide food. They said they had some food and provisions for the beginning but soon they would require help with provisions, obtaining supplies in the field, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what did you say to him in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: On following day I asked them what I should do. Every morning I have to inform my superior about the situation in the facility. I asked how I should act in this situation now that I was aware of what was at stake. The gentleman told me I should wait a little longer, and he told me when I should provide my information to my superior, and this is how things unfolded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you discussed accommodation, were you told anything about the duration of their stay at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you just go on accommodating them without knowing how long for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While we are on that particular subject, and this being the first visit, I'm going to ask you to describe, how long did this first visit at the hotel Rajac with General Mladic and his entourage, how long did that last?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Given all the time that has passed, I can't assess exactly how long it lasted. For a month, that would be the minimum, but maybe more. The time passed by rapidly because I was constantly on the move travelling. But maybe it was even two months, maybe it lasted for two months, but it certainly lasted for one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to an earlier answer that you gave, Mr. Gunj. You answered at page 21, I'm looking at starting at line 2, your answer was: "How should I handle this situation now that I was aware of what was at stake? And the gentleman told me that I should wait a little longer, and he told me that I should provide any information to my superior, and that is how things unfolded." So the question I want to ask you is, did he tell you you should provide information to your superior? Or did he tell you something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I think you've slightly misquoted the witness. I think the translation says: "... And he told me when I should provide my information to my superior."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My apologies. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, I misread the answer that is recorded. When did he tell you, or did he ever tell you when it was appropriate to tell your superior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No precise time was mentioned. He said I should wait for a few days, and he would then tell me that the situation was under control and that I didn't have to worry. And that is how I acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So after their arrival, was there a -- did you report to your superior the following day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No, I did not report to my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you first report to your superior after the arrival of General Mladic and his entourage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First of all, did you ever report at all? Did you report at all to your superiors at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I reported to my superior a few days later. I went on official trips to Belgrade on one or two occasions, and later I requested the authorisation to report to my superior so that he could be aware of what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And from whom did you seek that authorisation to report to your superior about the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Banduka for authorisation since I had most contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you ask Mr. Banduka for authorisation to report to your superior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I asked him for such authorisation almost every day, but I think that he said a few days later that I could report to my superior. I can't remember exactly how many days passed, but it wasn't long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, did you report General Mladic's visit to anyone else prior to reporting it to your superior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Because Mr. Jovanovic was my immediate superior, and I would only forward reports to him about the situation in the facility, because according to the chain of command, he was responsible for me and for the entire facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to the Judges the circumstances under which you did describe to -- was it Colonel Jovanovic, was that his rank? When it was that you reported to Jovanovic about the presence of Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I personally visited him in his office in Belgrade. We were alone. I told him everything I have just told you. I told him about the guests in the facility, and I told him about the ongoing activities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was his reaction or response?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: He was very much surprised and somewhat suspicious because I don't think he found it easy to believe that there were such things taking place in my compound. Given his reaction, I would say that he was not aware of the fact that these things were going on in my compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to change topics, and this would be a convenient time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll then take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, earlier in your evidence you testified that Lieutenant Banduka had informed you early in one of your earlier conversations that the provisions of food and water and supplies that were available to General Mladic were limited; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. A few minutes ago you testified about a discussion that you had with Lieutenant Banduka in which he informed you that the amount of food and the amount of drinks that were available to General Mladic and his entourage was limited. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He informed me that there was food and drink available for a brief period of time only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And since this stay was quite prolonged, you said a minimum of a month and possibly longer, what was the source of supplies of food and drinks to General Mladic and his entourage while he was staying at the hotel Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: For the first few days they had their own food drink they had brought with them. When they ran out of this, food and drink was bought on the market, and then supplies came from the resources of the army, from my unit. As time passed -- as time went on, the frequency increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say the frequency increased, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: As the supplies they had ran out, more and more supplies from my unit had to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I just want to understand something here. You said when the supplies ran out, they bought on the market, and then they got units -- supplies from your unit. How long did they buy from the market?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was combined. They used more than one source. They used what they had brought with them, and they also bought some. But as their own stocks decreased, they continued buying a little on the market, but more and more came from my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how did that -- the supplies from your unit, how were they procured and how were they delivered to General Mladic and his entourage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: To start with I received certain sums of money from them for articles I went out to buy on the market. Other supplies I picked up personally in my car in the Topcider warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To whom -- when supplies were needed did you requisition supplies from another source, from the army sources, or did you require or request supplies from any particular source in the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I went to Belgrade, and on the spot I took articles from the central warehouse. There was no written requisition form or anything like that. It was up to the people who were there to give me as much as they thought I needed. I'm referring to food stuffs and also material for personal hygiene and for cleaning the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was it standard operating procedure in the VJ to not have paperwork for requisitioned supplies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I only requisitioned the supplies orally. The people who issued them to me probably kept records. But I did not have to justify the supplies in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that standard operating procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: You mean under normal circumstances would that be the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No, no. It was not standard procedure. The standard procedure is quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the standard procedure, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: The standard procedure as regards the facility would be a requisition form for seven days for all the articles needed, and based on that requisition form, the articles and supplies would be issued, and daily documents would have to be filled in justifying the expenditure. And then at the end of the month all of the plus and minus parts of the column would have to be added up, and the condition, the situation, the state would have to be worked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why was there no paperwork kept under these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No records were kept because it was suggested to me that I

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (redacted) became acquainted with the situation and the events at the facility, he agreed and approved that gradually supplies should begin arriving, supplies of certain material, and that I should not keep any records of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me -- at the end of General Mladic, his stay and his entourage's stay at the hotel Rajac that we've been discussing, do you know where General Mladic went? And do you know the circumstances of his departure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I did not know then where he went, but the circumstances were the usual. It was nighttime, vehicles arrived, men. I didn't know where the gentleman was going to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you subsequently learn where he went?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you learn and from whom did you learn it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: When I arrived on official business in Belgrade to the Topcider barracks in Belgrade where my command is, I ran into certain people from Mladic's security who had been there with him, and chatting informally with them I found out that they occasionally went to Stragari and that Mladic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that confirmed to you by other sources as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: In February of the following year, the transfer of the general with part of his entourage was arranged again from Stragari to Rajac, and that was when I definitely learned that Mladic had been transferred from Rajac to there because he had come back now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did anybody in particular inform you that General Mladic and his entourage had been at Stragari?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No, those were the two sources. Nobody informed me officially, nor did anyone tell me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on how many other occasions, beside this long protracted visit we've been discussing, on how many other occasions was it that General Mladic and his entourage returned to the hotel in Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: They came back on two occasions in 1998 from Stragari to where I was, and they stayed there for a week because there was an eventful hunters being held in Rajac attended by many citizens, so evidently he couldn't be there. And the same happened the next year, 1999. And in 2000, I'm not sure whether he came or not, I think he did, but stayed only briefly. I'm not sure, as regards his coming there from Stragari. And in 1988, as the witness said, and 1989 I think, that's when he came again to the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, your statement as translated on the monitor says that, and I'm going to quote: "I'm not sure as regards his coming from Stragari. And in 1988 [as interpreted], as the witness said, and 1989 [as interpreted], I think, that's when he came again to the facility." Are those years that I've quoted accurate or inaccurate? 1988?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I think 1988 and 1989 are correct, but I'm not sure about 2000, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me -- the first time you observed General Mladic was in 1997, that was his first visit according to your earlier evidence.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The transcript as recorded says that his subsequent visits were in 1988, which is nine years before his first visit. So my question to you is -- my question to you is, is what appears on the transcript 1988 accurate or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No, no. It's an error. It's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What should it be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: It should be 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And you may have said this, but the duration of those visits, are you able to tell us the duration of each of those visits.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: As I've already stated, the visit in 1998 from Stragari to Rajac lasted up to about eight days. I think it was in late January or in February. I think it was February actually. And the following year it was the same. And in the year after, I'm not sure. But if he did stay, he stayed only for two or three days. The two brief visits in between were one-day visits only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, during those visits of General Mladic and his entourage, the subsequent visits, can you describe what the circumstances were with regard to the provision of food, drinks, and supplies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: The circumstances were the same as when he first came to stay. We provided food and everything else that was necessary for him to stay there for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: During those subsequent visits when you provided the food, was there paperwork maintained showing that food had been provided? Or was it the same as had occurred during the first visit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: The situation was the same as when he first came to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during these visits, these numerous visits that you've described, did General Mladic have visitors?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: You are referring to the visits from Stragari when he came back to visit Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, let me rephrase that question. During these subsequent visits, during the first visit and during the subsequent visits of General Mladic and his entourage to the hotel Rajac, did anyone visit General Mladic that you personally observed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: When he first stayed in the hotel, I observed and I know that General Curcin came to visit him. Later on Colonel Ljubisa Vukovic, who later was promoted to the rank of General; my commander, Colonel Jovanovic; and captain Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did -- during the subsequent visits, did he have other visitors beside those you've named?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: On about two occasions Mr. Ljubisa Beara was part of that entourage. That was the first time he was there, but he didn't show up when Mladic visited on later occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The transcript says Mr. Ljubisa Beara was part of that entourage. They don't say part of the visitors. Now, I don't know was he part of the entourage, and if it's part of the entourage, which entourage?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Gunj, was Ljubisa Beara a visitor? Or was he part of the Mladic's entourage that came and went from the hotel Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Ljubisa Beara was not in the entourage when Mladic first came to visit, but he arrived after awhile. However, judging by his actions and behaviour, I understood him to be part of that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Quite simply because Mr. Beara, as I saw, coordinated activities with Mr. Darko Pecanac as regards securing the facility, travel, and other things which I had no access to. But I concluded from the way they acted and talked that Mr. Pecanac was subordinated to him as regards security for the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And who was -- you mentioned a name -- you mentioned the name Darko Pecanac. Who was Darko Pecanac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Darko Pecanac was the security officer in General Mladic's entourage while he was staying in my facility. And he arrived as part of that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he have an accent that was particularly identifiable accent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, almost everyone had Bosnian accents. Almost all those people. Some had a stronger accent, others less strong, but they all did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see General Trajkovic who was the 1st Army commander come to your facility and visit General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I saw General Trajkovic. After awhile he came to visit General Mladic with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in addition, Mr. Gunj, to the visitors that you personally observed visiting to General Mladic, did you hear from other persons about the identities of visitors who had come to visit General Mladic while he was staying at the hotel Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, I heard from the people in General Mladic's security that while I was away, because I had to be away for periods quite often, the then Chief of General Staff Mr. Momcilo Perisic came to visit; and the then chief of the VVA, Mr. Aca Jovicic; and a little later a General of the of the Republika Srpska, Mr. Milan Gvero. This is information I learned from the security men, but I did not see them myself because I wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one other thing just to assist my colleague, we welcomed -- we have both -- correction, we have both statements in the e-court system so this can be called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine, I don't have it in the e-court system; I have a hard copy. So whatever is most convenient. If I can call -- if you could give me that number, Counsel, I would call it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a statement given to Judge Plazinic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D 005910.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, can you see on the monitor in front of you what is the first page of this -- an interview, what is described as an interview on the 6th of November, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with the assistance of the Registrar, if we could turn to the last page in the English and the last page in the B/C/S. Second to last page in the B/C/S, apparently. If we can go to the next page in the English. I'm looking to go to page 8 in the English version, please. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, perhaps Mr. Lukic can assist me because I don't read Cyrillic. But there's a paragraph that starts with: "After Perisic's visit to Mladic ..." It's on page 8 in the English version, and it is about mid-page. I can't direct the witness to where the Cyrillic passage starts if it's on that page at all, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I can see that. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in that statement to Judge Plazinic, does reading that passage refresh your recollection, Mr. Gunj, about the events that you've testified to here? In other words, did you inform Judge Plazinic, that after a visit to Mladic that you had heard about there was another visit when you were at the hotel when you were "sitting outside the hall and at one point Perisic came out of the hall and suggested to me that Mladic's stay at the hotel should not be spoken about much." Do you remember giving that statement to Judge Plazinic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. That's what it says here in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And last night or yesterday when you were being -- reviewing your evidence with me and with an investigator and an interpreter, did you have an opportunity to review the statement that was prepared after the session that was spent with me and with the investigator and the interpreter? Did you review a statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I did, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in that statement, Mr. Gunj, did you state that General Perisic visited Mladic at the hotel Rajac while Perisic was chief of the VJ General Staff. Mr. Gunj knew who Perisic was. Perisic spent a short time conversing with Mr. Gunj and told him not to spread information about what was happening and to take care not to spread information about Mladic's stay. Is that in a previous statement that was prepared last night as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I hadn't planned to introduce either one of these as an exhibit, but given that if I can -- I only have a hard copy, Your Honour. If I can produce a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you talking about this statement that you reviewed with the witness last night, that's what you are reading from, because you are not reading from the document before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I understand that, Your Honour. In other words, there are two previous consistent statements with his evidence before. The first I've shown you, Your Honour, the testimony before Judge Plazinic, this statement I have not put on the -- in the electronic system. I only have a hard copy, and I can only remind the witness with a hard copy and read verbatim from this statement and ask the witness if that's the statement that he made yesterday. And then I could, Your Honour, with the Court's permission, I could get this put into the electronic system, and we could give it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Things are done in reverse in this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I understand. I hadn't anticipated that we would get to this particular point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even then, shouldn't you discuss the fact of a statement with the witness first and tender that statement before you read it out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I'm at your disposal, Your Honour. I have a hard copy only. I do not have an electronic version. Since we are dealing with the electronic era --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the only copy you have is a hard copy. Then you say, Your Honours, I'm in this predicament, this is the only copy I have. Can I tender it? May I ask leave to tender this one before going into the content of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, then I stand corrected, Your Honour. If I could tender a copy of this statement in a hard copy to be followed by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you could do that. But you have told the witness the content of the statement. So it's water under the bridge now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand. He's signed this statement. It's a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm at your disposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead. Prosecute your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Gunj: I have a copy of a statement, a proofing note, information report, that you signed yesterday evening. Do you remember signing a proofing note yesterday evening?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prior to signing that proofing note, was the note reviewed by you with an interpreter, was it read back to you in a language you understood?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, the interpreter read out the entire statement to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, a portion of that statement reads as follows, and I would like you to use your recollection and affirm whether this is what was read out to you last night: "General Perisic visited Mladic at the hotel Rajac while Perisic was the chief of the VJ General Staff. Mr. Gunj knew who Perisic was. Perisic spent a short time conversing with Mr. Gunj and told him not to spread information about what was happening and to take care not to spread information about Mladic's stay." Do you remember that portion of the statement being read back to you before you signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to read another passage to you, and I'm going to ask you if this is what you recall was read back to you. Just give me a minute to find the passage. This is the passage I'd like to read to you. If you would either affirm or not confirm that this is what was read back to you before you signed this statement. There was a portion of this paragraph where you identified people who had come to visit General Mladic. And then the passage goes on, the paragraph goes on: "In addition to the visits of the persons identified above, which he personally observed, he heard from Mladic's security personnel that General Gvero had visited Mladic on another occasion as had General Perisic." Now, do you recall that portion being read back to you before you signed this particular information report?
