utterances.text: The one in the stamp in the upper left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: It's confidential number 1015-3 of the 25th of August, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I know, or rather, I know the general Momcilo Perisic, but I have never had the opportunity of seeing his signature on official documents. For this reason, I can't say that I recognise his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, this is a document that amends a previous decision issued by the VJ Chief of the General Staff, that is decision 1015-1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how does -- in what particular does this document identify -- in what way does this amend the previous order issued by General Perisic? THE COURT: The previous order issued by General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In what way does the document in front of you amend General Perisic's order of the 1st of July, numbered 1015-1?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I can't see it very well. Can we zoom in a little bit, please. The only amendment I see here is that the command of the 1st Army will report to the office on a monthly basis on the material issued and expended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you could go above that, you'll see an item number 3.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Procuring, issuing, and handing over of food stuffs and other expendable material referring to this decision, is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir. So is that the amendment to the previous order 1015-1 of the 1st of July in your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this whole line of questioning boils down to the reading of documents, and after that a leading question is put to the witness. I don't think we can get any facts out of this sort of testimony. THE COURT: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that regard, I am directing the witness's attention to certain portions of this document. Mr. Novak Lukic is correct on that, and what I would like to do is request that this document be marked for identification and then I will show the witness the next document as well, and then I intend to ask the witness about the collection of documents he has seen. So if this document, Your Honour, I take my colleague's point on that, if I could have this document marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think we've gone too far with marking documents for identification. The witness has only read something, he doesn't even recognise Mr. Perisic's signature, so how can we mark this document in this way? It's all boiling down to just reading the document without any sort of analysis. I think we've strayed too far from what we are supposed to be doing when tendering documents through a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but, Mr. Lukic, is the marking for identification not precisely to guard against that, so that if no further evidence and facts ever extracted, then it is not admitted. I thought your learned friend indicated earlier that there are five document that he would like to tender through this witness, all of which have a relationship. I'm not suggesting that that's how to establish a link between the witness and those documents. But I am just saying that is what he has said he wants to do, and when we raised the problem with the first document of those five, the solution was to mark them for identification. I'm not quite sure why you suddenly change now. You can't say because you have gone too far. That is a grounds for changing, can you? We have allowed it to go on, and now we can't change simply because it's gone too far. At least he is still within the five documents that he talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I accept your suggestion, Your Honour. And I agree that it be marked for identification. Sometimes we may become too emotional when objecting, and we say things we don't need to say as lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. May I ask that next time we try to reflect just for one moment before we stand up to say something. Then we'll admit this and mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P 618, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, while we are on this particular document, this document that is before you, you were a warrant officer -- you were a warrant officer at the time in July of 1997; is that correct? Or were you a senior sergeant in July of 1997 when you were the manager of the Rajac hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Are you referring to the year 1997?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I was then a staff sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And was it -- did you ever receive an order from the Chief of General Staff while you were a staff sergeant in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No, neither orally nor in writing. I received no order from the Chief of General Staff then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were the normal practices in terms of issuing orders? Was there a general practice where a particular sequence of orders would be issued?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes. The line of subordination was followed. The chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And so tell the Judges what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I would receive an order from my immediate superior, Colonel Jovanovic. Colonel Jovanovic would receive orders from the Chief of Staff of the 1st Army, or the commander of the 1st Army because he was subordinated to them, and the commander of the 1st Army would receive orders from the Chief of General Staff. That, in my opinion, was the chain of command that had to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gunj, I want to return back to the document that's in front of you, P 618 that has been marked for identification. It makes a reference to a decision 1015-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter number 9097, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, we can see from this particular document that it is dated the 1st of July, 1997. It's a decision of General Perisic, and I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 1 of the document which reads: "Issue the fuel for the replenishment of the Army of Republika Srpska vehicles on the basis of verbal authorisation from the Yugoslav Army Chief of General Staff at petrol stations in Belgrade as follows ..." It then identifies those stations. My first question is, what is a verbal authorisation in the context of the VJ? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: This means a subordinate may receive an oral order or approval from his superior in order to carry out an activity, and the superior will assess how far he is authorised to issue such an oral order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we have seen a series of documents that relate -- that start in the beginning of July, and conclude on the 27th of August, that relate to both the provision of petrol and the provision of food and moveables and other expendables. Can you -- having examined these documents, can you give us your view of these particular documents and what your impressions and what your conclusions are based on looking at these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness is being asked to speculate now. In his replies he did comment on all these documents; now he is being asked to give his impression. I don't think the question can be put in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll reframe the question, Your Honour. I'll be glad to reframe the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Please rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, do you draw any conclusions from the five documents that you have examined this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question has been rephrased, but the witness is still being asked to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can respond. The witness is a career military officer who testified in the context of a series of events that took place from the beginning of July that relate to people in the RS who stayed on his facility, that relates to the provision of food and other assistance. He is aware of the manner in which orders are given in the VJ. He was informed by his superiors that such provisions would be made available. He identified the normal procedures through which procurements of items was made in the course of events. And in my submission, Your Honour, he is in a position based on what he observed and what he heard, what he saw, and what he knows about orders in the VJ to give Your Honours his views on these particular documents. And I think, Your Honour, it's not speculation. I think he has a firm basis in which to make conclusions and draw conclusions after considering the complete context of the events and these particular documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly, Your Honour, Mr. Gunj is here as a fact witness and he has testified as to his knowledge of facts. With all due respect, Mr. Harmon is now asking the witness to interpret something that he, himself, said he has no direct knowledge of. The witness has come to testify to certain facts. And the documents put to him by Mr. Harmon are documents which Mr. Harmon was to have tendered through a different witness. I don't want to comment on that any further, but this witness is now being asked to comment on these documents, whereas he is here as a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, when you ask that these documents be marked for identification, I thought you were going to later call a witness who has a relationship with the documents and can testify to them positively, like an addressee or something like that. You know, I notice that even the documents that relate to the supply of food are not addressed to this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For me, I am afraid I share the view of the Defence on this point. And if you insist on these documents being admitted, then I'll are to confer with my colleagues. But based on the testimony thus far, I have still not seen the relationship between this witness and the documents. Now, I understand that he has testified about facts that happened during July 1997 at his facility, but he has not received any of these documents or he hasn't told us. So I don't see how if he wasn't the author, he didn't receive them, he hadn't seen them before he came to court, he saw them during proofing yesterday, how it can be said that there is a relationship between him and the documents, simply because he has testified about other facts that took place during the same period? That's the only link you are putting forward?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make a submission to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is a link to these documents. The document that amends -- that went to the 1st Army amending the previous document that said provide fuel, there was a document that amended that previous order that said, also include food articles, moveables, and other expenditures. That's 617 MFI. That document was received by Mr. Gunj's unit. By his superior command. That, Your Honour, Mr. Gunj was the implementer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He hasn't told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, he told Your Honours that he had gone to his Superior Command. He had authority to provide food, that food was provided on an increasingly more frequent basis. The man who -- the gentleman who was his superior officer was Mr. Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But if I may just remind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: According to his testimony, when he implemented those orders he had received oral orders, not written orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you more, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So he has not shown any link between himself and the written orders. He has told us, yes, he supplied food, but based on oral orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond quite respectfully, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The then sergeant Gunj wasn't in a position, he testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, but I don't think that this is a subject that we should be discussing in the presence of the witness. If any other questions might be put to the witness, if Mr. Harmon wants to provide us with an explanation, but nevertheless still has questions to put to the witness, I don't think it's fair to the witness to proceed in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe the best thing is to consult my colleagues, and we'll just rule. Do you still want to make submissions? In that event then the witness should stand out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I should conclude with my submissions, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Gunj, I'm sorry to do this. But this is what happens sometimes during trials. Could you please stand outside for a couple of minutes. We'll call you back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness was a staff sergeant or a sergeant. He was instructed -- or he informed his superior officer who was Jovanovic that Mladic was present at the facility that was under the control of the VJ. He told him about the provision of food. He would go back to Jovanovic to get food and provisions from the VJ to support General Mladic and his entourage. The orders that came down from the Superior Command went to sergeant Gunj's superiors. Sergeant Gunj was the implementer of what was -- had been ordered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have that evidence, Mr. Harmon. You haven't ask this witness that question. You haven't asked him whether he supplied any replenishments based on any of these written documents. He has testified that he did so based on oral instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They, quite obviously, Your Honour, will be gaps, but I think the Court is in a position to infer based on the evidence that these -- and I think it goes to weight. That, in the structured army like the VJ where there is a hierarchical command system, that all these orders from the Chief of General Staff would not going to Sergeant Gunj. And given the fact, Your Honour, that the presence of General Mladic on a VJ base was a highly sensitive matter, and sergeant Gunj has testified that he was instructed there should be no traces identifying that visit. It seems to me, and it's my submission, that Sergeant Gunj would not be the recipient of such orders. His superiors would be the recipient of such orders, and in the hierarchical command system, Sergeant Gunj who was in charge of that facility would be the person who would implement that, whether it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then would the appropriate witness not be sergeant Gunj's superior who will say, I, Sergeant Gunj's superior, received these written instructions and because the presence of Mladic in the area was a high secret, based on these written orders, I gave verbal orders to Gunj to implement these orders? Don't you see the missing link there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Of course I do, Your Honour. It's obvious. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you want us to jump --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want, Your Honours, I'm suggesting Your Honours can make an inference from the evidence that the orders are before Your Honours, the five orders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Applied to the situation that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you do know, Mr. Harmon, that the inference to be made must be the only reasonable inference. Cannot be one of many.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, it would my submission, Your Honour, that it is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from these orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting it's not a reasonable inference to infer that Gunj implemented the oral orders, and apart from those oral orders and in addition to them, further written orders came to other people? Isn't that -- wouldn't be that an equally reasonable inference to draw?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's my -- well, Your Honours could draw any inferences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is it not reasonable?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is an inference that can be drawn, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it not reasonable?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's a reasonable inference that can be drawn, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So there are more than one reasonable inferences that can be drawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously, weighing this evidence Your Honours have to give this evidence whatever weight Your Honours feel appropriate. What I've asked for -- we are at this point because I've asked this witness, who is a professional soldier, who was involved in the process of providing food and supplies to General Mladic, to give us his sense of these documents. Now, that's evidence that, in addition to any other witness who comes in, the Court, I think, should consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And shouldn't we await for that other witness to come in before we remove the MFI?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not asking to remove the MFI, Your Honour. What I was asking for was this witness to give us his sense of these documents. Now, it may be, Your Honours, it may be, Your Honours, in your deliberations you conclude that these five documents, based on the -- whatever answer he gives, the MFI should be removed. It also may be your position that you want to hear from somebody else who will also give you some input into these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'm very sorry then if you are not asking for the MFI to be removed. Can I just find out something from Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you rose on the point that the witness is now being asked to speculate. Whatever characterization the Chamber might give to that answer to the extent that these documents are still MFIed, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without going into whether the MFI marking will be removed at the request of the Prosecution, regardless of that, I object to this question which tries to get the witness to provide expert testimony. But is he a factual witness; he doesn't know anything about the documents. So I object to Mr. Harmon's questions in which he tries to obtain conclusions from the documents, but in any event, I do object to having these documents admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry we took long. By majority, Judge David descending, the objection is upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that case we can call the witness back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do we do with 9097?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that it also receive an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 9097 -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May it please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P 619, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I conclude, I have the previous document that I redacted portion of the information report that we discussed with Mr. Gunj's evidence. It has a document identification number 0646-6762. If that could be brought up on the screen, Your Honour. I have shown it to my colleagues from the Defence, and they have no objection in its present form to its admission. You will see if Your Honours go to the next page, you'll see those are the extracts of the information report that I read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You will see at the bottom of each page there is initials of the witness, and at the last page there is a signature and a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour, to tender it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P 620.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, I have finished my examination. I have no additional questions. Mr. Lukic from the Defence will now ask you questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Gunj, good day.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Novak Lukic. On behalf of Mr. Perisic's Defence team, I will now put some questions to you, but before I start, I'd like to warn you that since we both speak the same language, pause briefly after I put my question to you and then answer the questions so that the interpreters can follow us. You can also follow the cursor, rather the transcript to know when to answer.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you a few question that don't directly relate to what you have testified about, but it's in the interest of the Defence to obtain an answer. It's important for our case. You were born in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are a professional soldier, you joined the army in 1991 when you were in Rijeka; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I was to enter as an officer, as a professional officer, but I was [indiscernible] to the army there, but there was a problem when I joined the unit. The procedure was completed, and from 2002 to 2005 I was a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From 1992 to 1995 I assume, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's just one question I'd like to put to you about this in the course of the war up until 1995, you were in Army of Yugoslavia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: What do you mean during the war? When I came from the unit in the Republic of Croatia, I was in the unit of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you were in the JNA in Croatia. And then when the VJ, the Army of Yugoslavia was established, you became junior officer in the Army of Yugoslavia, and you remained there up until the present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that no one caused you any problems because you didn't go to fight in Croatia in the Serbian Army of Krajina, you stayed here all the time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. At page 78, line 12 and 13, it is supposed to be 1992 to 1995 or 1992 to 2005? I thought in 1997 he was still a professional soldier, that's why he was running the Rajac and all these other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Yes. I wanted to correct that error because he said in line 10, 2002 to 2005, that was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the correct answer is 1992 to 2005 [sic]. Thank you, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In fact you are still junior officer in the Army of Yugoslavia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Non-commissioned officer, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd now I'll like to put another question to you when answering Mr. Harmon's questions about the facilities, you mentioned the hotel in Topcider, and you said that there were some officers who is lived there with their families. Is it correct to say that the officers and their families lived there but they had come from the area of the former Yugoslavia, they lived there because they had no other accommodation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, some of the people who were there fell under that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Stragari facility that we have been discussing, when did you first go to the Stragari facility? Well, first I'll ask you, did you go to the facility in Stragari?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the period you have testified about. In 1997 and 1998 did you personally go to Stragari?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No. Before assuming my duties of the manager of the hotel in Rajac, I was assisting at a ceremony organised by the army command, and it was because of the day of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's spring 1997; isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1997 from the summer of 1997 when you became the manager of the facility in Rajac and in 1998, this is the period I'm interested in, during that period you didn't go to Stragari?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: In the course of 1998, no, I didn't go to Stragari.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you don't have any direct information on whether Mr. Mladic was there at the time, but as you have said, this is something that you heard from others?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Correct. What I said is what I heard, that I wasn't personally present when these activities were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to ask you this. Mr. Harmon asked you a question about this entire event, towards the end of June you were appointed as the manager of the Rajac facility. That was in 1997; have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what you told Mr. Harmon about Mr. Mladic's stay in Rajac in the facility, well, according to you, this took place in July during 30 days in July 1997?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning of July. That's when these activities commenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this because I received your personal file, we'll call it up on the screen, but perhaps there are a few things you could explain to see whether there are any problems, but you were appointed as the manager of the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the following document up on the screen. 1D 005927. Page 4. Unfortunately, Your Honours, I only have the B/C/S version of this document that we received in one of the most recent batches of documents provided by the Prosecution. Could we just scroll down a little bit, and then I will read out, very slowly, what it says in the last column in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is this, you say this is his personal file.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Personal file or personnel file?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We can also have the first page on the screen, it's his personal file. We can have a look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All non-commissioned officers had such a document, and this is your document. This is your personal file; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at page 4 now, please. And let's have a look at the last part. Could we enlarge that or zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first column has to do with the situation of the active member of the military, I'll read out what it says. It says, "manager of the military hotels Topcider and Rajac." And then it says HQ administration, second column which concerns the unit and the institution, it says 1A. I assume that means the 1st Army Belgrade garrison. The third column it says, and this concerns the establishment rank, it says "SVLK." That's staff sergeant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: That's a staff sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 22401 PG-18/18. I don't know whether you can help us to understand what this stands for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: It's the rank grouping, the salary grouping.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then it says period, 1st of August, 1997, up until the 28th of August, 2002. And in the last column it says the decree regulating the situation 1A, 12-48, date, the 19th of May, 1997. Have I read this out correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is, did you arrive on the 1st of August to the Rajac hotel when you were appointed its manager? Or do you abide by your statement that this was in July?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Well, there are two pieces of information which are incorrect here. One is my rank. I was a staff sergeant at the time. I became a staff sergeant 1st class when I was promoted during the bombing. So that's the first item that's incorrect. And, secondly, it's not true I was appointed on the 1st of August, 1997. I was in fact appointed on the 1 st of June, 1997. So those two pieces of information are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you think that information here is not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: I'm sure of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to make sure that those of us who don't read B/C/S have it clear, can it be placed on the record what those dates are for, 1st of August 1997 to 28 February -- June, 2002. And is this the time when he was employed in that capacity as manager of these two hotels?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like confirmation from the witness himself. Do those columns, sir, are they supposed to signify the date when you assumed your duties as the manager of those two hotels until the day when you finished doing so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. It should be the day when I took over, that's the 1st of June, early June. And the day when I ended my duty there, that can't be correct because I was still doing that job then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We understand that. You say the entry is wrong. But we just wanted to know what those two columns designate so we know what we are talking about. You may continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I suggest that pages 1 and 4 be MFIed until we get the official translation of this page. Then when you have all the information from the form, it will be complete, and I think you will come across such documents often in the course of the trial. So for now, I propose that it be MFIed until we get official translation of this document, or if Your Honours feel it's understandable based on the transcript, it need not be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see Mr. Harmon gives a look and doesn't do anything. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D 55, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, you said when asked by Prosecutor Harmon that you knew from the media at the time that Mr. Mladic was indicted before The Hague Tribunal. That this information was already been broadcast in the media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you had this information from the media not along your professional line?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No, nobody informed me officially or gave me any guide-lines in that respect. I knew that only from the sources I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just please slow down a little bit. Do you agree with me that at the time in the media it was said that our state leadership did not want to extradite anyone to The Hague Tribunal because there was no law on cooperation with the Tribunal and this was the policy of the state leadership and that this was often explained in the media.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that at that time, although everybody knew that General Mladic had been indicted before the ICTY, he was often seen in public and that this was published in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Are you referring to the period before he came to the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Both before and after, did you hear that he was seen in public?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, did I hear that, and I did see that in the media, but nobody ever gave me any official information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about what you saw in the media.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to put a question to you concerning your testimony of today, and it's also mentioned in the statement you made before Judge Plazinic. And I think that this is document 1D 005910.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that Exhibit P 614?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. Let me just see what page I need. I do apologise. I think I would like first to see the previous statement, 1D 005924, page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't want us to see the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid we don't have this document in English, Your Honours. I received this document from Mr. Harmon, but it's not in the 65 ter list of documents. I will read a sentence to the witness, but I don't intend to tender this statement. Can we scroll up a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this passage you describe your first meeting with Mr. Mladic, and you say something here which I didn't hear today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't have a sufficient identification on what document this is that we are referring to. Is it -- is there a date on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this was before the investigating judge of the second municipal court in Belgrade on the 24th of March, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, this has been provided to the Defence in English as well, so there is an English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to come to your colleague's rescue now that he says he doesn't have an English version

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have a -- let me -- if I could have the usher -- the assistance of the usher, the usher could give this to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has it been uploaded on the system; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To my knowledge, it hasn't, Your Honour. This was not going to be an exhibit offered by the Prosecution. So we gave a copy of this in English and B/C/S to the Defence. I can give a copy of the English version to Mr. Lukic, and if he wants to reference a particular passage, it might assist him and assist me at least in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Harmon. It's my mistake exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to read a sentence to the witness. But, Witness, after what you said that somebody rang you up on the telephone while you were still in Belgrade and they said they were from the office of the Chief of General Staff, my question is from that moment onwards, did anyone ever contact you in the same way, ring you up, whether in Rajac or in Topcider saying they were calling from the office of the Chief of General Staff the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: You mean me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this statement, when you say the following: "When I arrived at the facility I saw people in civilian clothes with weapons and later on it turned out that these were the security guards of Ratko Mladic. A man approached me. I went with him to the entrance of the hotel. And at the entrance I met Ratko Mladic. It was clear it to me what this was about. After this I asked Ratko Mladic's security guards for an explanation, and they said that I would learn everything from the General Staff." And so on and so forth. That's what it says in this record. That's why I asked you whether someone spoke to you like this and whether you were told that someone from the General Staff would call you, but you say that nobody called you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ
utterances.text: It's true they told me someone would ring me up, but no one did. Apart from that first instance which I have described when somebody said they were calling from the office but didn't introduce themselves. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't wish to tender this document. And, Your Honours, we have two minutes left, but I think that it's a convenient moment now to break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Sir, we are not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in page 20, line 14, you were asked by the Prosecution: "Was that a standard operating procedure?" And you answer: "You mean under normal circumstances would that be the procedure? "No, no. It was not standard procedure." You answer: "The standard procedure is quite different." Then question in line 19: "Can you describe the standard procedure, please." And you answer: "The standard procedure as regards the facility would be a requisition form for seven days for all the articles needed ..." and you describe all of this. My question to you is this: Do you recall in your experience in the administration any other incident or circumstances in addition to the one of the stay of General Mladic in which all the written procedures were not required? Do you recall in your experience, I repeat, other incidents or circumstances in addition to the one you have just described, in which written procedures were not followed, which is to say, the requisition forms and so on? Please elaborate, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never came across such a situation. This was the only time. In every other situation the standard procedure was followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, we have not finished with your testimony. You will have to come back tomorrow again at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in the same courtroom. You are warned not to discuss this case with anybody for as long as you are still giving evidence, so overnight you can chat about the weather but not about the case to anybody including counsel for the Prosecution. Okay. You may --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may stand down, we'll see you tomorrow afternoon at quarter past 2.00 in the same courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The court stands adjourned to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
